title: Bēowulf
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 39–42, lines 1050–1124 (fitt XVI). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Ðā gȳt ǣghwylcum eorla drihten
þāra þe mid Bēowulfe brimlāde tēah,
on þǣre medubence māþðum gesealde,
yrfelāfe, ond þone ǣnne heht
golde forgyldan, þone ðe Grendel ǣr
māne ācwealde, —
sentences.l: Then still to each of the earls, the lord, of those who with Beowulf drew the sea-way, on that mead-bench gave treasure, heirloom, and bade that one man be paid for with gold, him whom Grendel before wickedly killed, —
sentences.i: Then the lord gave further treasure on the mead-bench, heirloom-gifts, to each of the earls who had made the sea-crossing with Beowulf, and ordered gold to be paid in compensation for that one man whom Grendel had wickedly killed before, —
sentences.n: The sentence runs on through several verbs: ‘gesealde’ (gave) governs ‘māþðum’ (treasure, accusative singular) and ‘yrfelāfe’ (heirloom, accusative singular in apposition), and the dative ‘ǣghwylcum’ (‘to each’), with ‘eorla’ (genitive plural, ‘of the earls’), says who received them; ‘drihten’ (lord) is Hrothgar, the subject. ‘Ðā gȳt’ is ‘then moreover’. ‘heht … forgyldan’ is ‘bade … be paid for’ (‘ordered’ in the idiomatic version): ‘heht’ is the past of ‘hātan’ with an infinitive, and ‘forgyldan’ means ‘to repay, requite with gold’, a wergild, the blood-price that settles a killing. ‘þone ǣnne … þone ðe Grendel … ācwealde’ is ‘that one … the one whom Grendel killed’; the poem does not name him here; the man is presumably the Geat of Beowulf’s band whom Grendel killed in Heorot (a Geat called Hondscio is named much later, at line 2076, but nothing in this passage says he is the man meant). ‘māne’ is an adverb, ‘wickedly’, from ‘mān’, ‘crime’ (the same root as ‘mānscaða’ in the house table). ‘brimlāde tēah’ is ‘drew the sea-way’: ‘brimlād’ is ‘sea-way’, a compound of ‘brim’ (surf, sea) and ‘lād’ (way, journey), and ‘tēah’ is the past of ‘tēon’, ‘to draw, lead, go’, so ‘drew the sea-way’ is a literal and slightly odd picture of making the voyage; I take it as ‘made the crossing’, which is a guess at the idiom. Klaeber’s italic ‘ā’ is his change: the manuscript has ‘leade’, and Kemble read ‘-lāde’. The apparatus also has the entry ‘Fol. 153a fe lafe’, which seems to give the manuscript’s own reading of ‘yrfelāfe’ on that leaf (folio), but the shorthand is terse and I do not build on it. The final dash sets the next clause beside this one.

sentences.t:
swā hē hyra mā wolde,
nefne him wītig God wyrd forstōde
ond ðæs mannes mōd.
sentences.l: as he of them more would [kill], unless wise God had withstood the fate for them, and that man’s mind.
sentences.i: as he would have killed more of them, had not wise God withstood the fate for them, and the purpose of that creature.
sentences.n: ‘swā hē hyra mā wolde’ is ‘as he would [kill] more of them’: ‘mā’ (more) takes the genitive ‘hyra’ (of them), and the infinitive ‘ācwellan’ is left out and has to be supplied from the line before. ‘nefne’ is ‘unless’ and takes the subjunctive ‘forstōde’ (past subjunctive of ‘forstandan’, ‘to withstand, prevent’), so the sentence says what would have happened without God. ‘him’ is a dative of interest, ‘for them’, and the two things God withstood are ‘wyrd’ and ‘ðæs mannes mōd’. ‘wyrd’ is ‘fate’, the course events were taking, and ‘ðæs mannes mōd’ is ‘that man’s mind’. I take ‘mannes’ as Grendel, called ‘man’ in the old sense of any person; it is a guess, and a reader could also take it as Beowulf, whose courage joined God in the work. ‘wītig’ is ‘wise, knowing’. The poet steps aside here, as he does in several places, to say that the outcome was God’s doing as much as Beowulf’s.

sentences.t:
Metod eallum wēold
gumena cynnes, swā hē nū gīt dêð.
sentences.l: The Measurer ruled over all of the race of men, as He still does now.
sentences.i: The Lord ruled all mankind, as He rules it still.
sentences.n: ‘Metod’ is ‘Measurer’, the old name for God used in the house rendering (see Fitt I, line 109); it comes from ‘metan’, ‘to measure’, the one who metes out. ‘wēold’ is the past of ‘wealdan’, ‘to rule’, which takes the dative or genitive: ‘eallum’ (dative, ‘over all’) with ‘gumena cynnes’ (‘gumena’ genitive plural, ‘cynnes’ genitive singular: ‘of the race of men’; ‘guma’ is a poetic word for ‘man’). ‘swā hē nū gīt dêð’ is ‘as he now yet does’: ‘dêð’ is the present of ‘dōn’, ‘to do’, with a circumflex, Klaeber’s mark for a contracted vowel, and it stands for ‘wealdeþ’, ‘rules’. The tense shifts from past to present because the poet is speaking to his own day, a Christian audience, about a story set in heathen times.

sentences.t:
Forþan bið andgit ǣghwǣr sēlest,
ferhðes foreþanc.
sentences.l: Therefore is understanding everywhere best, forethought of the spirit.
sentences.i: So understanding, the mind’s forethought, is best in every case.
sentences.n: ‘Forþan’ is ‘therefore’ and ties the saying to the last unit: God turned the fate aside, so wisdom, not luck, is the thing to prize. ‘bið’ is the habitual present of ‘bēon’ (‘is, is always’), the tense of proverbs. ‘andgit’ is ‘understanding, intelligence’ (nominative, the subject), ‘ǣghwǣr’ is ‘in every case, everywhere’, and ‘sēlest’ is the superlative ‘best’. ‘ferhðes foreþanc’ is ‘forethought of the spirit’: ‘ferhð’ is the mind or inner self, and the phrase restates ‘andgit’ in other words. Whether this is the poet’s maxim or a general truth he borrows, it is the first of two short sayings before the story starts.

sentences.t:
Fela sceal gebīdan
lēofes ond lāþes sē þe longe hēr
on ðyssum windagum worolde brūceð!
sentences.l: Much must he experience of the dear and of the hateful, he who long here in these wind-days enjoys the world!
sentences.i: Much, both of the loved and the hated, must he live through who long has the use of the world in these days of wind!
sentences.n: ‘Fela’ (much) is the object of ‘gebīdan’ (to live through, experience), and the genitives ‘lēofes ond lāþes’ (‘of the dear and of the hateful’) say what the much consists of: joy and harm alike. ‘sceal’ is ‘must’. ‘sē þe’ is ‘he who’, the subject of ‘sceal’ and, inside the relative clause, of ‘brūceð’, and ‘brūcan’ takes the genitive, so ‘worolde’ is ‘of the world’: he who has the use and enjoyment of the world. ‘windagum’ is ‘wind-days’, a compound of ‘wind’ and ‘dagum’ (days); I take it as the windy, changeable days of this life, as opposed to the lasting days of the next, and that is a guess from the parts. ‘on ðyssum’ is ‘in these’. The exclamation mark is Klaeber’s. The saying is a warning that sets up the sorrow of the tale: a long life holds loss as well as gain, and Hildeburh is the case in point.

sentences.t:
Þǣr wæs sang ond swēg samod ætgædere
fore Healfdenes hildewīsan,
gomenwudu grēted, gid oft wrecen,
sentences.l: There was song and sound together at once before Healfdene’s battle-leader, the joy-wood greeted, a lay often recited,
sentences.i: There was singing and music together before Healfdene’s war-leader, the harp was struck, and a tale was told, many times over,
sentences.n: ‘Þǣr wæs sang ond swēg’ is ‘there was song and sound’; ‘samod ætgædere’ is two words for ‘together’ piled up. ‘fore’ is ‘before, in front of’, with the dative ‘hildewīsan’ (‘battle-leader’, from ‘hilde’, battle, and ‘wīsa’, leader). ‘Healfdenes hildewīsan’ is ‘Healfdene’s battle-leader’, and the person meant is Hrothgar, Healfdene’s son, so the phrase names him by his father. The apparatus shows scholars unhappy with the line: Lübke adds ‘[suna]’ (son), Möller would read ‘ofer’ (‘concerning’) for ‘fore’, and one editor prints ‘Hrōðgāres’ for ‘Healfdenes’. ‘gomenwudu’ is ‘joy-wood’, a kenning for the harp; the participles ‘grēted’ (‘greeted’, that is, the strings struck) and ‘wrecen’ (‘recited’, from ‘wrecan’, ‘to drive, utter’) have no ‘wæs’, which has to be supplied. ‘gid oft wrecen’ is ‘a lay often recited’, and the apparatus gives ‘eft’ (‘again’) for ‘oft’ to Lübke and Trautmann.

sentences.t:
ðonne healgamen Hrōþgāres scop
æfter medobence mǣnan scolde,
[be] Finnes eaferum, ðā hīe se fǣr begeat.
sentences.l: when the hall-joy Hrothgar’s scop along the mead-bench was to tell, [about] Finn’s descendants, when the sudden peril seized them.
sentences.i: whenever Hrothgar’s poet, along the mead-bench, was to give the hall its entertainment with the tale of Finn’s descendants, and of how the sudden disaster seized them.
sentences.n: ‘ðonne’ is ‘when, whenever’, and with ‘scolde’ (‘was to, had to’) it describes what the singer did on each such evening. ‘healgamen’ is ‘hall-joy’, the entertainment of the hall, and is the object of ‘mǣnan’ (‘to tell of, recite’, a verb that can also mean ‘to lament’). ‘scop’ is the court poet (see Fitt VII, line 496), and ‘æfter medobence’ is ‘along the mead-bench’, the row of seated drinkers. In Klaeber’s text ‘[be]’ is a word Thorkelin added: without it ‘Finnes eaferum’ is a bare dative, and with it the sense is ‘about Finn’s descendants’. The apparatus lists other fixes: ‘eaferan’ (another form of the same word), Trautmann’s ‘gefēran’ (companions), and editors who think a line has dropped out before 1068. ‘eafera’ is ‘offspring, heir’, and who exactly are Finn’s ‘eaferan’ is uncertain, so ‘descendants’ is a guess. ‘ðā hīe se fǣr begeat’ is ‘when the sudden peril seized them’ (‘fǣr’, a sudden attack or danger; ‘begeat’ from ‘begietan’, ‘to get hold of’), and ‘hīe’ is ambiguous: it may mean Finn’s ‘eaferan’ themselves or the Danes who fought them, depending on how ‘eaferum’ is read, and the poem is only recalling a story the hall already knew.

sentences.t:
Hæleð Healf-Dena, Hnæf Scyldinga,
in Frēswæle feallan scolde.
sentences.l: The hero of the Half-Danes, Hnæf of the Scyldings, in the Frisian-slaughter was to fall.
sentences.i: The champion of the Half-Danes, Hnæf of the Scyldings, was fated to fall in the Frisian slaughter.
sentences.n: These are the first lines of the tale itself, and it opens with the doomed man: ‘Hæleð Healf-Dena, Hnæf Scyldinga’ is two phrases in apposition, ‘the hero of the Half-Danes, Hnæf of the Scyldings’, and ‘scolde’ (‘was to, was fated to’) gives the sense of destiny. ‘Healf-Dena’ is ‘of the Half-Danes’, a people or a branch of the Danes whom Hnæf leads; the name’s exact meaning (a half-share of the Danes, or the people of ‘Healfdene’) is a guess. The apparatus records that Grundtvig and Kemble print ‘Healfdenes’, ‘Healfdene’s [hero]’. ‘in Frēswæle’ is ‘in the Frisian-slaughter’, with ‘wæl’ (slaughter, the field of the slain) and ‘Frēs-’ (Frisian); it could be the name of the battle or of the place, and I take it as the battle. Hnæf is Hildeburh’s brother, as the lines about his pyre show (1114–1117).

sentences.t:
Nē hūru Hildeburh herian þorfte
Ēotena trēowe;
sentences.l: Not at all indeed had Hildeburh need to praise the Eotens’ good faith;
sentences.i: Hildeburh had certainly no need to praise the good faith of the Eotens;
sentences.n: ‘Nē hūru’ is ‘certainly not’, and ‘þorfte’ (past of ‘þurfan’, ‘to need’) with ‘herian’ (‘to praise’) means ‘had need to praise’. ‘Ēotena trēowe’ is ‘the Eotens’ good faith’, the accusative ‘trēowe’ with the genitive plural ‘Ēotena’. The line is a litotes: the poet says she had no cause to praise their loyalty, and means they had betrayed it. Who the ‘Ēotan’ are is disputed: they have been taken as the Jutes or as another name for Finn’s people, whom the text also names Frisians (‘Frēsena’, ‘Frȳsna’). The word is spelled like ‘eotenas’ (ogres) at Fitt I, line 111, and some scholars take it as the same word. Hildeburh, as the lines will show, is a Danish princess married into Finn’s house, and the Eotens are her husband’s side.

sentences.l: guiltless was she bereft, at that linden-play, of dear children and brothers;
sentences.i: without guilt she lost, in that battle, her dear children and brothers;
sentences.n: The skeleton is ‘wearð beloren’ (‘was bereft’, passive of ‘beleosan’, ‘to lose’), which takes the dative of what is lost: ‘lēofum bearnum ond brōðrum’ (‘of dear children and brothers’; ‘lēofum’ is the adjective, agreeing with both nouns). The subject is Hildeburh, carried over from the last unit. ‘unsynnum’ I read as an adverbial dative of ‘unsyn’, ‘guiltlessness’, ‘guiltlessly’, but it is a difficult word: the apparatus shows editors changing it to ‘unsynnig’, ‘unsynnigum’ and ‘unsyn(n)gum’ to make a plain adjective, so call my reading a guess. ‘lindplegan’ is ‘linden-play’, a kenning for battle: ‘lind’ (linden, the wood of shields) and ‘plega’ (play). Klaeber’s italics mark his change: the manuscript has ‘hild-’ (‘battle’; the apparatus gives only this first element), and Kemble read ‘lind-’; the sense is nearly the same. ‘Sweorda gelāc’, ‘sword-play’, at Fitt XV line 1039 is the same kind of image: war as a game. ‘bearnum ond brōðrum’ names her children and brothers together; the poem has not said how many of each.

sentences.t:
hīe on gebyrd hruron
gāre wunde;
sentences.l: they at birth fell, wounded by spear;
sentences.i: they fell, as fate had set it, wounded by the spear;
sentences.n: ‘hīe … hruron’ is ‘they fell’ (past plural of ‘hrēosan’), and ‘gāre wunde’ is ‘wounded by spear’: ‘gāre’ is the dative of means, ‘wunde’ the participle. The unclear phrase is ‘on gebyrd’: ‘gebyrd’ is ‘birth, lineage’ and, in some uses, ‘fate’, and neither reading is certain. I chose ‘as fate had set it’, a guess; ‘by birth’ in the sense of ‘as kinsmen, by the claims of blood’ is the other possibility. The apparatus also has an entry ‘Fol. 153b wunde AB’; I take it to concern the manuscript’s own reading of ‘wunde’, but the shorthand is terse and I do not build on it. The semicolon runs the sentence on to the exclamation.

sentences.t: þæt wæs geōmuru ides!
sentences.l: that was a sorrowful lady!
sentences.i: Sorrowful woman that she was!
sentences.n: ‘geōmuru’ is the nominative feminine of ‘geōmor’, ‘sad, mournful’, and ‘ides’ is the poetic word for a lady of rank (see Fitt IX, line 620, ‘ides Helminga’). ‘þæt’ is the neuter pronoun used for ‘that one’, as the poem often does for a person it pities. The exclamation mark is Klaeber’s, and the words are the poet’s cry.

sentences.t:
Nalles hōlinga Hōces dohtor
meotodsceaft bemearn, syþðan morgen cōm,
sentences.l: Not at all without cause did Hoc’s daughter bewail the Measurer’s decree, after morning came,
sentences.i: With good cause did Hoc’s daughter mourn the Lord’s decree, after morning came,
sentences.n: ‘Nalles hōlinga’ is ‘not at all without cause’, another understatement for ‘with very good cause’; ‘hōlinga’ is ‘in vain, without cause’. ‘Hōces dohtor’ is ‘Hoc’s daughter’, so Hildeburh is named by her father, a way the poem identifies a woman by her line. ‘bemearn’ is the past of ‘bemurnan’, ‘to mourn over’, with the accusative ‘meotodsceaft’. That compound is ‘Measurer-shaping’, the decree or ordained fate: ‘meotod’ (see Fitt I, line 109) and ‘sceaft’ (creation, decree). Her mourning is aimed at the decree itself, not only at the men who killed her kin. ‘syþðan morgen cōm’ is ‘after morning came’, the daylight that showed her the dead.

sentences.t:
ðā hēo under swegle gesēon meahte
morþọrbealo māga,
sentences.l: when she under the sky could see the murder-bale of kinsmen,
sentences.i: when she could see, under the open sky, the murderous destruction of her kin,
sentences.n: ‘ðā’ is ‘when’; ‘meahte’ is ‘could’, with the infinitive ‘gesēon’ and the object ‘morþorbealo māga’: ‘morþor’ is ‘murder’, ‘bealo’ is ‘evil, destruction’, and ‘māga’ is the genitive plural of ‘mæg’, ‘kinsman’, so ‘murder-bale of kinsmen’ means the killing of her relatives. ‘under swegle’ is ‘under the sky’ (‘swegl’), an old way of saying ‘in the open’. The dot under the ‘ọ’ in ‘morþọrbealo’ is Klaeber’s sign that this vowel does not count in the metre; it is a mark for readers of the verse and does not change the sense. The same sign appears again in this part, at ‘fēaụm’ and ‘meðẹlstede’.

sentences.t:
þǣr hē[o] ǣr mǣste hēold
worolde wynne.
sentences.l: where she before had held the greatest world’s joy.
sentences.i: where she had once held the greatest joy the world gave.
sentences.n: ‘þǣr’ is ‘where’, and ‘ǣr’ is ‘formerly’. ‘mǣste … wynne’ is ‘greatest joy’, with ‘wynne’ the accusative and ‘worolde’ the genitive, ‘of the world’ or ‘in the world’; the poem means the kin she lost, who were her greatest happiness. Klaeber’s ‘hē[o]’ is his addition: the manuscript has ‘he’, and the bracketed ‘o’ makes the feminine ‘hēo’ (‘she’), so the sentence stays with Hildeburh. Chambers keeps ‘hē’ and starts a new sentence with ‘Þǣr hē’, so the subject would be someone male, a reading the apparatus records and that I treat as less likely. ‘þǣr’ looks back to her kin: ‘where’ means ‘among whom’.

sentences.t:
Wīg ealle fornam
Finnes þegnas nemne fēaụm ānum,
sentences.l: War took away all Finn’s thanes, except for a few alone,
sentences.i: The fighting took off all Finn’s thanes but a few,
sentences.n: ‘Wīg’ (war, the fight itself) is the subject of ‘fornam’ (past of ‘forniman’, ‘to take away, destroy’), and ‘ealle … þegnas’ is the object, ‘Finnes’ the genitive, ‘of Finn’. ‘nemne’ is ‘except’ and takes the dative, so ‘fēaụm ānum’ is ‘a few only’. The dot under the ‘ụ’ in ‘fēaụm’ is the metre sign explained at line 1079, and the manuscript has ‘feaū’, with a mark over the ‘u’, which I take as the usual scribal sign for ‘m’; Klaeber writes the ‘m’ out. The few survivors are the people who survived the battle on Finn’s side, not Hengest’s; the lines that follow suggest that both sides were worn down, which is why a truce is offered.

sentences.t:
þæt hē ne mehte on þǣm meðẹlstede
wīg Hengeste wiht gefeohtan,
nē þā wēalāfe wīge forþringan
þēodnes ðegne;
sentences.l: so that he could not at the meeting-place fight war at all against Hengest, nor by war push the survivors away from the prince’s thane;
sentences.i: so that he could not fight a battle against Hengest at all on that field of meeting, nor by fighting drive the survivors from the prince’s thane;
sentences.n: ‘þæt hē ne mehte’ is ‘so that he could not’, a result clause, and ‘hē’ is Finn. ‘meðẹlstede’ is ‘meeting-place’ (‘meþel’, assembly, and ‘stede’, place), here the battle-ground; the dot under the ‘ẹ’ is the metre sign. ‘wīg Hengeste wiht gefeohtan’ is the hard part: ‘gefeohtan’ takes ‘wīg’ as its object (‘to fight a fight’), ‘Hengeste’ is dative (‘against Hengest’) and ‘wiht’ is ‘at all’. The apparatus lists other readings: Grein joins ‘Wīg-Hengeste’, Rieger puts ‘wiht Hengeste wið gefeohtan’, Holthausen reads ‘wiþ’ for ‘wiht’; my version is one reading, and the difference is slight. ‘wēalāfe’ (‘survivors’, a compound with ‘lāf’, what is left; the first element is ‘wēa’, woe, or ‘wæl’, slaughter, and I have not settled which) are the surviving Danes; ‘forþringan’ is ‘to push forth, dislodge’; ‘þēodnes ðegne’ is ‘the prince’s thane’, presumably Hengest, Hnæf’s man. Brown wants the plural ‘ðegna’ (the apparatus), which would make it all the prince’s thanes. The lines that follow treat Hengest as the leader of the Danish survivors.

sentences.t:
ac hig him geþingo budon,
þæt hīe him ōðer flet eal gerȳmdon,
healle ond hēahsetl,
sentences.l: but they offered terms to them, that they should clear to them another hall completely, hall and high-seat,
sentences.i: but they offered them terms: that they would clear another hall entirely for them, hall and high-seat together,
sentences.n: ‘ac’ is ‘but’, and ‘hig’ is an old spelling variant of ‘hīe’ (they; Finn’s side). ‘geþingo’ (accusative plural, ‘terms, conditions’) is the object of ‘budon’ (‘offered’). The ‘þæt’ clause says what the terms are, with ‘gerȳmdon’ a past subjunctive, ‘would clear, make room’. ‘ōðer flet eal’ is ‘another hall completely’ (‘flet’, the floor, the hall itself), and ‘healle ond hēahsetl’ spells out what is given over: hall and chief seat. The grammar of the pair is awkward and the whole passage is one of the known problems of the Finnsburg story, since the next lines say the two sides were to share, so whether Hengest got a whole second hall or half of the same one is disputed. This is my reading, and a guess.

sentences.t:
þæt hīe healfre geweald
wið Ēotena bearn āgan mōston,
sentences.l: that they might own power over half, with the sons of the Eotens,
sentences.i: and that they might hold power over one half, alongside the sons of the Eotens,
sentences.n: ‘þæt hīe … āgan mōston’ is ‘that they might own’, with ‘mōston’ (‘were allowed to’, past subjunctive of ‘mōtan’) and ‘āgan’ (‘to own, possess’). The object is ‘geweald’ (‘power, control’), and ‘healfre’ is the genitive, ‘of half’, so ‘healfre geweald’ is ‘control of a half’. ‘wið Ēotena bearn’ is ‘with the sons of the Eotens’. The apparatus lists ‘healfne’ (accusative masculine) from several editors (Thorkelin, Trautmann, Holthausen, Sedgefield), which would agree with ‘geweald’ and give ‘half the power’ instead of ‘power over a half’. The meaning is the same in outline: the two sides would hold the hall in common.

sentences.t:
ond æt feohgyftum Folcwaldan sunu
dōgra gehwylce Dene weorþode,
sentences.l: and at the treasure-giving Folcwalda’s son every day honored the Danes,
sentences.i: and that Finn, son of Folcwalda, would honor the Danes with gifts every day,
sentences.n: The sentence stays inside the terms of the treaty: ‘ond’ joins this to the ‘þæt’ clause above. ‘Folcwaldan sunu’ is ‘Folcwalda’s son’, the poem’s way of naming Finn (Folcwalda means ‘ruler of the folk’), and he is the subject of ‘weorþode’ (‘honored’), with ‘Dene’ (the Danes, accusative) as object. ‘æt feohgyftum’ is ‘at the treasure-giftings’, with ‘feoh’ (cattle, wealth) and ‘gyft’ (gift), and ‘dōgra gehwylce’ is ‘of days each’, a genitive plural, ‘every day’. The past tense is the old form of the subjunctive ‘would honor’ and is the same as the plain past, so the sense comes from the clause around it.

sentences.t:
Hengestes hēap hringum wenede
efne swā swīðe sincgestrēonum
fǣttan goldes, swā hē Frēsena cyn
on bēorsele byldan wolde.
sentences.l: would delight Hengest’s troop with rings, just as much with treasure-possessions of plated gold as he would embolden the Frisian kin in the beer-hall.
sentences.i: and cheer Hengest’s troop with rings, just as lavishly with treasures of ornamented gold as he would hearten the Frisian kin in the beer-hall.
sentences.n: ‘Hengestes hēap’ is ‘Hengest’s troop’, the object of ‘wenede’ (past subjunctive of ‘wenian’, ‘to accustom, entertain, indulge’; ‘would delight’ is a guess at the shade), and ‘hringum’ is a dative of means, ‘with rings’. ‘efne swā swīðe … swā’ is the correlative ‘just as much … as’, which compares what the Danes receive with what Finn gives his own men. ‘sincgestrēonum fǣttan goldes’ is ‘with treasure-possessions of plated gold’: ‘sinc’ is treasure, ‘gestrēon’ is a thing gained, and ‘fǣttan’ is the weak genitive singular of the adjective ‘fǣtt’, agreeing with ‘goldes’, which I take as ‘ornamented, plated’, a guess. ‘Frēsena cyn’ is ‘the kin of the Frisians’, and ‘byldan’ is ‘to embolden, encourage’. The point of the clause is that the Danes are promised equal treatment with Finn’s own people. ‘bēorsele’ is ‘beer-hall’, the hall where the drink flowed.

sentences.t:
Ðā hīe getrūwedon on twā healfa
fæste frioðuwǣre.
sentences.l: Then they pledged on both sides a firm peace-covenant.
sentences.i: Then they made a firm pact of peace on both sides.
sentences.n: ‘Ðā’ is ‘then’, and ‘hīe’ is both parties. ‘getrūwedon’ is the past plural of ‘getrūwian’, ‘to pledge, make a compact’, with the accusative ‘frioðuwǣre’, ‘peace-covenant’, a compound of ‘frioðu’ (peace) and ‘wǣr’ (a pledge, treaty). ‘on twā healfa’ is ‘on two halves’, that is, ‘on both sides’. ‘fæste’ is ‘firm’. The apparatus here only cross-refers (‘See 669b Varr.’) to the variants listed at line 669b; I cannot say what point it makes for this line.

sentences.t:
Fin Hengeste
elne unflitme āðum benemde,
sentences.l: Finn to Hengest, resolutely, without strife, declared with oaths
sentences.i: Finn declared to Hengest, earnestly and with solemn oaths,
sentences.n: ‘Fin’ is the nominative of Finn’s name, ‘Hengeste’ is dative (‘to Hengest’), and ‘benemde’ is ‘declared, named solemnly’, the past of ‘benemnan’; ‘āðum’ is the dative plural of ‘āð’ (oath), ‘by oaths’. ‘elne’ is ‘with zeal, resolutely’. The doubtful word is ‘unflitme’, which occurs nowhere else in Klaeber’s text (the apparatus sends the reader to line 1129 for a similar word); I take it as ‘un-’ plus a form of ‘flīt’ (strife) and render ‘without strife’, meaning ‘without dispute, unwaveringly’. It is a guess, and the apparatus lists the editors’ trials: Grundtvig ‘unhlytme’, Trautmann ‘unslāwe’ and ‘unblinne’ (‘not slack’, ‘unceasing’) and Holthausen ‘unslitne’ (‘unbroken’). The apparatus also has an entry ‘Fol. 154a be’; I take it to concern the manuscript’s reading at ‘benemde’, but the shorthand is terse and I do not build on it.

sentences.t:
þæt hē þā wēalāfe weotena dōme
ārum hēolde,
sentences.l: that he would hold the survivors in honor, according to the counsellors’ judgment,
sentences.i: that he would treat the survivors with honor, by the judgment of the counsellors,
sentences.n: The oath has several clauses, each with ‘þæt’. ‘þæt hē … hēolde’ is ‘that he would hold’, a past subjunctive; ‘þā wēalāfe’ (the survivors) is the object; ‘weotena dōme’ is ‘by the judgment of counsellors’ (‘wita’, a counsellor or wise man, with ‘dōm’, judgment, in the dative); and ‘ārum’ is the dative plural of ‘ār’, ‘honor, mercy’, so ‘hold … with honors’ means ‘treat honorably’. The text does not say whose counsellors they are; they are presumably Finn’s.

sentences.t:
þæt ðǣr ǣnig mon
wordum nē worcum wǣre ne brǣce,
nē þurh inwitsearo ǣfre gemǣnden,
sentences.l: that there any man by words or deeds should not break the treaty, nor through malice-craft ever make mention of it,
sentences.i: that no man there should break the treaty by word or deed, nor ever through cunning malice bring the old quarrel up,
sentences.n: ‘ǣnig mon’ is ‘any man’ and the negatives ‘ne’ and ‘nē’ make it ‘no man’; this is normal in Old English, where double negatives add force. ‘wordum nē worcum’ is ‘by words nor by works’, the two ways of breaking faith. ‘wǣre’ is the accusative of ‘wǣr’ (treaty, pledge), and ‘brǣce’ is a subjunctive of ‘brecan’, ‘to break’. ‘inwitsearo’ is ‘malice-craft’ (‘inwit’, malice, and ‘searo’, device, craft), meaning treacherous cunning. ‘gemǣnden’ is a plural subjunctive of ‘gemǣnan’, ‘to mention, speak of’, and the shift from singular ‘brǣce’ to plural ‘gemǣnden’ is odd; I take it as a loose shift to ‘they’ (the Frisians), and the exact sense of ‘gemǣnden’ is a guess. ‘gemǣnden’ has no stated object; the next clause suggests it is the old killing, so I supply ‘the old quarrel’ in the idiomatic version.

sentences.t:
ðēah hīe hira bēaggyfan banan folgedon
ðēodenlēase, þā him swā geþearfod wæs;
sentences.l: though they followed their ring-giver’s slayer, lordless, when to them so need was;
sentences.i: even though they followed the slayer of their ring-giver, lordless as they were, when necessity so compelled them;
sentences.n: ‘ðēah’ is ‘though’. ‘bēaggyfan banan’ is ‘their ring-giver’s slayer’: ‘bēaggyfa’ (a lord who gives rings, a regular name for a king), ‘bana’ (killer), with ‘bēaggyfan’ genitive and ‘banan’ dative (the object of ‘folgedon’), so the one now followed is the lord’s killer. ‘folgedon’ is ‘followed’, in the sense of ‘served’, and takes the dative. ‘ðēodenlēase’ is ‘prince-less’ (‘ðēoden’, prince, and ‘-lēas’), the Danes who have lost Hnæf. ‘þā him swā geþearfod wæs’ is ‘when to them so it was needful’; ‘geþearfian’ is impersonal, ‘it was necessary’. This is the cost of the treaty in one line: men serve their lord’s killer, because they cannot do otherwise. The semicolon leaves the thought open for the next clause.

sentences.t:
gyf þonne Frȳsna hwylc frēcnan sprǣce
ðæs morþorhetes myndgiend wǣre,
sentences.l: if then any of the Frisians with bold speech should be a reminder of that murderous hate,
sentences.i: if then any one of the Frisians, with reckless talk, should remind them of that murderous hatred,
sentences.n: ‘gyf þonne’ is ‘if then, if ever’, and ‘wǣre’ is a subjunctive, ‘should be’. ‘Frȳsna hwylc’ is ‘any of the Frisians’, ‘ðæs morþorhetes’ is a genitive, ‘of that murderous hatred’ (‘morþor’, murder, ‘hete’, hatred), and ‘myndgiend’ is ‘one who reminds’ (an agent noun, ‘mind-giver’), which takes the genitive. ‘frēcnan sprǣce’ is the instrumental ‘with bold, reckless speech’: ‘frēcne’ is ‘bold, daring, dangerous’. Klaeber’s italic ‘an’ is his change: the manuscript has ‘frecnen’, and Thorkelin read ‘frecnan’ and Grein ‘frēcnan’. Trautmann and Holthausen print ‘myndgend’ for ‘myndgiend’, as the apparatus says; the sense is unchanged.

sentences.t: þonne hit sweordes ecg sēðan scolde. —
sentences.l: then the sword’s edge should settle it. —
sentences.i: then the edge of the sword should settle it. —
sentences.n: The clause says what would happen if a Frisian reminded the Danes of the killing: ‘þonne’ is ‘then’, ‘hit’ is ‘it’ (the matter), ‘sweordes ecg’ is ‘the sword’s edge’, the subject, and ‘scolde’ is ‘should’. The verb is a crux. The manuscript has ‘syððan’ (‘afterwards’), which does not fit, so Klaeber’s italic ‘ē’ makes it ‘sēðan’: I take it as ‘to prove, make good’ (from ‘sōð’, true), and from there ‘settle’ in the sense ‘decide’; that last step is a guess. The apparatus lists the other attempts: ‘sehtan’ (settle, reconcile), ‘sēman’ (decide), ‘swȳðan’ (overcome), ‘scȳran’ (cut) and a gap after ‘scolde’; Schücking thinks ‘myndgian’ is understood. This is a disputed reading, and what I give is a guess based on the sense of the whole clause. The final dash marks the break between the treaty and the funeral.

sentences.t:
Ād wæs geæfned, ond icge gold
āhæfen of horde.
sentences.l: The pyre was made ready, and [?]-gold was lifted up from the hoard.
sentences.i: The pyre was made ready, and gleaming gold was brought out of the hoard.
sentences.n: ‘Ād wæs geæfned’ is ‘the pyre was prepared’ (passive of ‘geæfnan’, ‘to perform, make ready’), and ‘āhæfen’ is the participle of ‘āhebban’, ‘to lift’. Klaeber’s italic ‘d’ in ‘Ād’ is his change: the manuscript has ‘að’, which most editors read as ‘āð’ (oath), and Grundtvig read ‘ād’ (pyre), which suits the lines that follow. ‘icge’ is the real puzzle: the manuscript has ‘⁊ icge’, and the apparatus lists Kemble’s ‘īcge’ (‘vegetus’, lively), Singer’s ‘incge’, Bugge’s ‘ondīege’ (openly), Holthausen’s ‘īdge’ (‘īdig’, resplendent) and ‘ītge’ (cf. Old Norse ‘itr’, splendid) and his ‘īcge’ (eagerly). No reading is certain, and ‘gleaming’ is a guess based on the best of them. The ‘hord’ is the treasure store, and the gold is taken from it for the burning.

sentences.t:
Here-Scyldinga
betst beadorinca wæs on bǣl gearu.
sentences.l: Of the Army-Scyldings the best of battle-warriors was ready for the pyre.
sentences.i: The foremost of the Danish warriors was ready for the pyre.
sentences.n: ‘Here-Scyldinga’ is ‘of the Army-Scyldings’, the Danes, genitive plural; ‘betst beadorinca’ is ‘best of battle-men’, with ‘betst’ (superlative ‘best’) and ‘beadorinca’ (genitive plural of ‘beadorinc’, ‘battle-warrior’). ‘wæs on bǣl gearu’ is ‘was ready for the pyre’ (‘on’ with the accusative ‘bǣl’ gives motion onto it). The poem does not give the man’s name here, but line 1114 says ‘Hnæfes āde’, so he is presumably Hnæf.

sentences.t:
Æt þǣm āde wæs ēþgesȳne
swātfāh syrce, swȳn ealgylden,
eofer īrenheard, æþeling manig
wundum āwyrded;
sentences.l: At the pyre was easy to see the blood-stained mail-shirt, the all-golden swine, the iron-hard boar, many an atheling destroyed by wounds;
sentences.i: At the pyre lay in plain sight the bloodstained mail-coat, the boar all of gold, the boar of hard iron, and many a noble brought low by his wounds;
sentences.n: ‘wæs ēþgesȳne’ is ‘was easy to see’ (‘ēþgesȳne’ is the predicate adjective), and the things that were easy to see follow as its subjects: ‘syrce’ (mail-shirt) is described as ‘swātfāh’ (‘blood-stained’; ‘swāt’, blood or sweat, and ‘fāh’, stained), ‘swȳn ealgylden’ is ‘swine all-golden’ and ‘eofer īrenheard’ is ‘boar iron-hard’. The boars are probably helmet-crests, or helmets bearing them (compare ‘eoforlīc’, ‘boar-image’, at Fitt IV, line 303), but the line does not say so, and the two phrases might even describe one boar-helmet, gilded and iron-hard. ‘æþeling manig’ is ‘many an atheling’ (‘æþeling’, a prince or man of noble birth), and ‘wundum āwyrded’ is ‘ruined by wounds’, from ‘āwyrdan’, ‘to destroy, injure’ (a guess at the exact shade).

sentences.t: sume on wæle crungon!
sentences.l: some in the slaughter fell!
sentences.i: Some had fallen in the slaughter!
sentences.n: ‘sume’ is the plural of ‘sum’, ‘some’, and ‘crungon’ is the past plural of ‘cringan’, ‘to fall, die’ (the usual word for dying in battle), so ‘on wæle’ is ‘in the slaughter’. The pluperfect ‘had fallen’ in the idiomatic version reflects the point in time, since the deaths came before the pyre. The exclamation mark is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
Hēt ðā Hildeburh æt Hnæfes āde
hire selfre sunu sweoloðe befæstan,
bānfatu bærnan, ond on bǣl dôn
ēame on eaxle.
sentences.l: Hildeburh then bade at Hnæf’s pyre her own son to the fire commit, the bone-vats burn, and put on the pyre, at his uncle’s shoulder.
sentences.i: Then Hildeburh ordered her own son to be given to the flames at Hnæf’s pyre, his body burned, and set on the pyre at his uncle’s shoulder.
sentences.n: ‘Hēt’ is ‘bade’ (past of ‘hātan’, as in ‘hēt secgan’ at Fitt VI, line 391), followed by three infinitives: ‘befæstan’ (‘to commit’, with the dative ‘sweoloðe’, ‘to the heat, to the flame’), ‘bærnan’ (‘to burn’), and ‘dôn’ (‘to put’, the circumflex being Klaeber’s sign for a contracted vowel, as in ‘dêð’ above). ‘hire selfre sunu’ is ‘her own son’ (‘selfre’ is the genitive of ‘self’, ‘of herself’); Thorkelin and Grein read ‘suna’ (sons, plural), and the apparatus notes this. ‘bānfatu’ is ‘bone-vats’, a kenning for the body (a vessel that holds the bones); the plural is probably poetic, and I give the singular in the idiomatic version. ‘ēame on eaxle’ is ‘to the uncle, on the shoulder’: Klaeber’s italic ‘ēa’ is his change from the manuscript’s ‘earme’ (‘arm’), made by Holthausen and Sedgefield, and ‘ēam’ is the mother’s brother, here Hnæf, so the boy lies at his uncle’s shoulder. Thorkelin read ‘axe’ (ashes) for ‘eaxle’, and Boer ‘earm ond eaxle’ (arm and shoulder), as the apparatus says. The reading with ‘ēame’ is a guess.

sentences.t:
Ides gnornode,
geōmrode giddum.
sentences.l: The lady grieved, lamented with songs.
sentences.i: The lady grieved, and mourned in songs of lament.
sentences.n: ‘Ides’ (lady) is the nominative subject, with the two verbs ‘gnornode’ and ‘geōmrode’, past tenses of ‘gnornian’ and ‘geōmrian’, both ‘to mourn’; the second restates the first. ‘giddum’ is the dative plural of ‘gid’, ‘a song, a lay’: the same word as in 1065, so she sings her lament as the scop sang the tale.

sentences.t: Gūðrinc āstāh.
sentences.l: The war-man ascended.
sentences.i: The warrior went up.
sentences.n: This is a disputed place. ‘Gūðrinc’ is ‘war-man’, ‘warrior’ (nominative singular) and ‘āstāh’ is the past of ‘āstīgan’, ‘to ascend, go up’. The literal sense is a man going up, perhaps onto the pyre, but it is not clear what is meant, and I give it as a guess. The apparatus shows the editors’ struggles: Grundtvig and Rieger read ‘gūðrēc’ (‘war-smoke’; cf. 3144), which would be ‘war-smoke went up’, and fits the next line well; Grein ‘gūðhring’ (‘clamor’, or ‘spirals of smoke’ as Sedgefield takes it); Scherer and Boer ‘gūðrincas tāh’ (‘the warriors went’). Klaeber keeps ‘Gūðrinc’, and so do I.

sentences.t:
Wand tō wolcnum wælfȳra mǣst,
hlynode for hlāwe;
sentences.l: The greatest of slaughter-fires wound to the clouds, roared before the mound;
sentences.i: The mightiest of death-fires wound up to the clouds and roared before the mound;
sentences.n: ‘Wand’ is the past of ‘windan’, ‘to wind, curl’, used for the climbing smoke or flame; ‘tō wolcnum’ is ‘to the clouds’ (dative plural of ‘wolcen’). ‘wælfȳra mǣst’ is ‘the greatest of slaughter-fires’: ‘wælfȳr’ is ‘slaughter-fire’ (‘wæl’, slaughter, ‘fȳr’, fire), a pyre for the slain, and the genitive plural with a superlative means ‘the greatest of all such fires’. ‘hlynode’ is ‘roared, resounded’, and ‘for hlāwe’ is ‘before the mound’; ‘hlāw’ is a barrow or hill, and the mound is presumably the one raised over the pyre’s remains, though the text does not say. Grundtvig and Trautmann read ‘from’ for ‘for’ and Holthausen ‘hrāwe’ (corpse), as the apparatus records. ‘wælfȳra mǣst’ is the subject of ‘wand’ and ‘hlynode’ whichever reading of the previous half-line is taken.

sentences.t:
hafelan multon,
bengeato burston, ðonne blōd ætspranc,
lāðbite līces.
sentences.l: heads melted, wound-gates burst, when blood sprang out, the hateful bite of the body.
sentences.i: heads melted, wounds burst open, when the blood leapt out, the foul gash of the flesh.
sentences.n: ‘hafelan’ is the nominative plural of ‘hafela’ (head); ‘multon’ is the past plural of ‘meltan’ (melt); ‘bengeato’ is ‘wound-gates’, a kenning for the openings of wounds (‘ben’, a wound, and ‘geat’, a gate), which ‘burston’ (‘burst’), presumably from the heat. ‘ðonne blōd ætspranc’ is ‘when blood sprang out’. ‘lāðbite līces’ is ‘hateful bite of the body’: ‘lāð’ (hateful) and ‘bite’ (a bite, a wound cut by a blade), with ‘līces’ the genitive of ‘līc’ (body). The unit’s last words stand alone in Klaeber’s punctuation, as an apposition to ‘bengeato’ or to ‘blōd’. The apparatus notes that many editors drop the comma and join ‘ætspranc’ to ‘lāðbite’: ‘the blood sprang from the hateful wound of the body’; Schücking says otherwise. I find the second reading the smoother.

sentences.l: Flame swallowed up all, the greediest of spirits, of those whom war took of both peoples;
sentences.i: The flame, greediest of spirits, swallowed all of those whom the battle had taken from both peoples;
sentences.n: ‘Līg’ is the subject, ‘forswealg’ the past of ‘forswelgan’ (‘to swallow up’) and ‘ealle’ the object. ‘gǣsta gīfrost’ is ‘greediest of spirits’, a phrase in apposition to ‘Līg’: ‘gǣst’ is ‘spirit, ghost’, and the fire is imagined as a ravening spirit, as a person would be. ‘þāra ðe þǣr gūð fornam’ is ‘of those whom the war took there’: a partitive genitive plural with a relative clause, with ‘gūð’ (war) as the subject and ‘fornam’ as the verb used earlier at 1080. ‘bēga folces’ is ‘of both peoples’ (‘bēga’ is the genitive plural of ‘bēgen’, both; ‘folces’ is genitive singular): the Danes and the Frisians are burned together.

sentences.t: wæs hira blǣd scacen.
sentences.l: their glory was departed.
sentences.i: Their glory had departed.
sentences.n: ‘wæs … scacen’ is the old perfect with ‘wæs’ and the participle of ‘sceacan’, ‘to depart, go away’, meaning ‘had gone’. ‘blǣd’ is ‘glory, prosperity, bloom’, and ‘hira’ is ‘their’, of the dead of both peoples. This half-line closes the fitt. The ‘blǣd’ that departed is the strength and fame both peoples had held before the fighting.
